thread.title: Sumrall has memorable moment to extend Bassmaster Elite career
thread.title_full: Sumrall has memorable moment to extend Bassmaster Elite career

author: Don Shoopman
title: Sumrall has memorable moment to extend Bassmaster Elite career
text:
CLAYTON, N.Y. – That a 6-pound bass reduced a tough, personable and proud family man to tears underscores the highest of highs Caleb Sumrall reached mid-afternoon Aug. 28 far from his home in New Iberia.
Sumrall, trying desperately to prolong his professional bass fishing career that has stretched nine years, needed that bass on the second day of the Lowrance Bassmaster Elite on the St. Lawrence River, the final regular-season tournament that would decide the fate of several Elites. After all, there was a 2 ½-pounder that needed to be culled out of his boat’s livewell.
The New Iberian rose to the occasion like he did two weeks earlier with a Top 10 finish at Lake Champlain out of Plattsburgh, N.Y. He set the hook and got his hands on a bass nearly three times bigger than his smallest bass in the waning minutes of Day 2 to give him 24 pounds, 9 ounces, for a two-day total of 47 pounds, 12 ounces.
Sumrall, who was fishing to save his chosen and hard-earned livelihood, caught more clutch bass on Day 3 to finish 36th with 70 pounds, 3 ounces, and collect $5,500. It was worth so much more than that because it was the key to extending his career.
Sumrall’s final total of 425 points left him in 69th place in the Angler of the Year standings. If he would have finished below 70th his nine-year Elite career would have come to an end.
He was 77th in 2025. Based on the relegation system, he’ll be able to drop two subpar years after 2027.
The 39-year-old all-around outdoorsman and charter boat captain was happy for himself, his wife, Jacie, and their children Clelie and Axel, other family and friends and a growing legion of supporters.
“It was a really trying last couple of years. Nothing seemed to click,” he said.
Caleb Sumrall smiles as he holds a giant novelty check in each hand on Aug. 27, Day 1 of the Bassmaster Elite tournament in New York on the St. Lawrence River. They signify the Phoenix Big Bass and Rapala CrushCity Monster Bag honors he won two weeks earlier at the Bassmaster Elite on Lake Champlain in New York. His big bass of the tournament weighed 6 pounds, 10 ounces, for $1,000 and his big limit weighed 24 pounds, 4 ounces, worth another $2,000.
bassmaster.com
However, Lake Champlain, one of his favorite bodies of water in the Northeast, sparked a fire in him during a tournament in which he had the biggest bass and the heaviest one-day weight total.
It was all on the line two weeks later on Day 2. He had that “small” smallie to get rid of.
At the weigh-in, Sumrall told the crowd he was about out of gas, about out of ideas and about out of spots. He was about out of time, too, because it was 2:45 p.m., the hour of reckoning close at hand with five bass weighing approximately 20 ½ pounds finning around in his livewell.
Bassmaster Elite Series tournament emcee Dave Mercer, right, interviews Caleb Sumrall on Day 2 of the 2026 Lowrance Bassmaster Elite at Clayton, N.Y. Sumrall’s results Aug. 27-30 turned out to be one of the “feel good” stories of the season as he fished into Semifinal Saturday, finished 36th overall to win $5,500 and, more importantly, finish 69th in the AOY race to avoid his pro bass fishing career coming to an end.
bassmaster.com
As he faced the mic and Bassmaster Elite tournament emcee Dave Mercer, Sumrall described the sequence of events and said, “I hit one spot right before takeoff (about 2 miles from Clayton Harbor Municipal Marina) and I caught a 5-13 (actually 6ish) and made a 3-pound cull and I have never been so emotional about a fish catch than at that time. I’m not going to lie to y’all. I cried in the boat like a baby. I do not care. It was actually my most memorable, favorite fish catch I’ve ever had, ever,” he said on the big stage, repeating the last word of the last sentence for emphasis.
While Sumrall drove his Toyota pickup truck and Xpress boat home, the talk centered around that big, beautiful smallmouth bass and the events leading up to it on Aug. 28, which could have been his last day as a bass pro.
“It was a fight. Day 2, you know. I knew I needed anything north of 23 ½ pounds to make it to Day 3, and it was pretty stressful. I only had 21 pounds before I caught that big one. I was thinking I was going to get cut. I was fighting hard,” he said as he drove across the Mississippi countryside, still 4 hours from home.
“I ran all over trying to make something happen. I had that little one I had to get rid of. I caught the big one. That was a career-saving fish.”
Sumrall said that big bass was in about 6 foot depths on a small, rocky point with grass on it. It was a place he targeted three or four times and caught several fish that hit the digital scale manned by Bassmaster Elite tournament director Lisa Talmadge on Day 1.
He saw the bass on LiveScope.
“I couldn’t really tell how big she was till she came up. It’s hard to tell between a 3 ½ and 6-pounder there,” he said.
A “good ol’ Coike ball,” watermelon seed-colored, was on the business end of his fishing rod, he said. He made one cast, the “hawg” bit and he boated it to ensure moving into the Top 50.
Bassmaster Elite Series tournament manager Lisa Talmadge, left, holds a weigh-in bag Aug. 28 for Caleb Sumrall to return the big smallmouth bass he caught Day 2 of the 2026 Lowrance Bassmaster Elite tournament at Clayton, N.Y. His clutch catch in the waning minutes before weigh-in pushed him into Semifinal Saturday, where he fished well enough to finish 36th and requalify for his 10th year as an Elite.
facebook.com
“That one meant the most to me when it counted. Like I said, it was a whirlwind of emotions. I knew that was my best chance” to qualify for Semifinal Saturday and get another chance to avoid the grim reaper called relegation.
Day 3 loomed big, obviously. He admitted he really was “in a better place mentally” than he was on the second day.
Still, Sumrall had to put the right size bass in the Xpress powered by a Yamaha 250-h.p. Sho.
“I ran Lake America,” he said, referring to the former Lake Ontario renamed by the Trump Administration. “I hit a bunch of stuff. It was a good start.”
He put nearly 9 pounds in the boat with two keepers before 9 a.m. About one hour later he hooked and boated a 5-5.
“I had three good ones. I knew I needed two more decent bites. I think at 2 o’clock I had two 3-pounders in the box,” he said, noting that size wouldn’t cut it, particularly if one died because it couldn’t be culled.
“Then I lost a couple really big ones. That kind of hurt,” he said.
“Then I ran back to the river with an hour to go and hit the same spot (where he caught the miraculous 6 a day earlier) to catch two 4-pounders to give me enough weight to finish in the 30s. It was like a ton of weight was lifted off my shoulders. I figured I wasn’t going to drop weight (and lose place in the standings).”
After his pressure-packed days Aug. 27-30 on the St. Lawrence River, Caleb Sumrall is looking ahead to more years on the Bassmaster Elite Series circuit. His 36th-place overall finish was enough to prevent the New Iberian from being relegated from the Elites.
facebook.com
That didn’t happen. He’ll enter his 10th season as an Elite in 2027.
“I want to win one for everybody rooting me on. I want to win one for my family. You can’t win one if you’re not there, so that’s the goal next year,” he said.
He tipped his cap to his wife and children.
“I wouldn’t be able to do it without them. They’re my biggest support system. Jacie’s holding it down. I’ve been on the road for a month. It means a lot,” he said.
He’ll resume guiding in and around Vermilion Bay, probably in about two weeks, he said. His new saltwater boat is being delivered this week and he’ll be rigging it up for the fall saltwater fishing season … safe in the knowledge he has a professional bass fishing career to tend to in ’27.
